title: Fundamentals: Philosophy, Execution Model, and Portability
description: How Python, Java, and C differ in design philosophy, execution model, and portability.
objectives: Compare the three languages' design goals and typical use cases
Understand what portability means differently for each

content.heading: Python
content.body: Python prioritizes developer productivity and readability above raw performance. It's interpreted (via CPython bytecode) rather than compiled to native machine code, which makes it slower for CPU-bound work but extremely fast to write, test, and iterate on. Typical use cases: scripting, data science, web backends, automation, and rapid prototyping.

content.heading: Java
content.body: Java prioritizes portability ('write once, run anywhere') and robustness for large, long-lived applications. It's compiled to platform-independent bytecode, then executed by a JVM that JIT-compiles hot paths to native code at runtime — a middle ground between fully interpreted and fully compiled. Typical use cases: enterprise backends, Android apps, large-scale distributed systems.

content.heading: C
content.body: C prioritizes direct hardware control and predictable performance, with almost no runtime overhead or built-in safety net. It compiles directly to native machine code for a specific target architecture — no virtual machine, no bytecode. Typical use cases: operating systems, embedded firmware, device drivers, and performance-critical libraries other languages build on top of.

content.heading: Key Differences
content.body: Execution model is the core distinguishing axis: C compiles straight to native code; Java compiles to bytecode run by a JVM; Python is interpreted from source (via an intermediate bytecode, invisibly, in CPython). Portability means different things: C source is portable if you recompile it per platform; Java bytecode itself is portable, running unmodified on any compatible JVM; Python source is portable as long as a compatible interpreter is available. Safety vs. control is the other major axis: C gives you the most control and the least protection (manual memory management, no bounds checking); Java and Python both manage memory automatically and provide much stronger runtime safety, at the cost of some performance and low-level control.

content.heading: When It Matters
content.body: Choosing among them is rarely 'which is objectively best' — it's about matching tradeoffs to the problem: C when you need to work close to the hardware or squeeze out maximum performance; Java when you need portability, strong tooling, and robustness for a large team/codebase; Python when development speed and readability matter more than raw execution speed.

keyPoints: C compiles to native code; Java compiles to portable bytecode run by a JVM; Python is interpreted from source
Portability is achieved differently: recompiling C, running Java bytecode anywhere, or running Python source anywhere a compatible interpreter exists
C trades safety for control; Java and Python trade some performance/control for memory safety and productivity
